h1: Setting a responsible service policy for drunk guests
title: Responsible Service Policy for Brewpubs | Craft Beer School
desc: How to write a responsible service policy for a brewpub: spotting intoxication, refusing service calmly, getting guests home and logging incidents.
teaser: Every brewpub will have a guest who has had enough. The policy decides whether that night ends quietly.
standfirst: Refusing a drink is the hardest conversation on a bar floor. A written policy takes the guesswork away from a 22 year old server on a Saturday night. Here is what ours would say.
sections: Why a written policy beats good judgement

Most brewpubs leave it to whoever is behind the bar. That means one server cuts a guest off and the next one serves him two more pints. The guest learns to ask someone else. The staff learn that refusing is optional.

A written policy fixes that. It says what the brewpub expects, who has the final word and what happens next. It protects the guest, the staff and the licence. Excise and police rules on serving intoxicated people vary by state and change, so check your licence conditions and the current state rules, then make your policy at least as strict.
Know the signs, not just the pint count

Counting drinks is a poor guide. A 9% imperial stout and a 4% session lager are very different pints. Body weight, food and pace all change how fast people get drunk. Train staff to watch behaviour instead:

  • Speech: slurred, loud or repetitive.
  • Movement: swaying, stumbling, spilling drinks, fumbling with a phone or wallet.
  • Mood: sudden aggression, crying, arguments with friends or staff.
  • Judgement: buying rounds for strangers, trying to drive, wandering into the brewhouse.

Write ABV on the tap list for every beer. Make sure servers know which beers on it are strong. A guest drinking 8% beers at the same speed as lagers needs watching sooner.
A traffic light system staff can actually use

We like a simple three stage system because it gives staff a step before refusal:

  • Green. Guest is fine. Normal service.
  • Amber. Early signs. Slow the pace: offer water and food, suggest a lower ABV beer or a smaller serve, let the shift manager know.
  • Red. Clearly intoxicated. No more alcohol. The manager handles the conversation.

Amber is where most nights are saved. A glass of water put down without asking, a plate of something salty and a half pint instead of a full one often settle a table before anyone needs to say no. Our guide to choosing serve sizes shows why a smaller serve on the menu helps here.
How to say no without starting a fight

The refusal itself should be short, private and calm. The manager, not the youngest server, delivers it. A good script sounds like this: "I am not able to serve you more alcohol tonight. Can I get you a water, a soft drink or something to eat?" No lecture, no debate, no accusing the guest of being drunk in front of his friends.

Offer something in return. A soft drink, food or a call to a cab gives the guest a way to save face. Bring a sober friend from the group into it. Never let a refused guest just be passed to another bar station.

India's drink driving limit is 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood. One or two strong beers can put a guest over it. The policy should say plainly that staff will not hand car keys to a guest who is visibly drunk and will offer to book a cab or a driver.

Keep a list of local driver services at the bar. Make the cab offer part of the closing routine on busy nights. Some brewpubs keep a parking arrangement so a guest can leave a car overnight without penalty. Make the safe choice the easy one.
Design the menu and the promotions around the policy

A policy on paper can be undone by the menu. Bottomless beer deals, shot challenges and "finish the tower" offers all push guests to drink fast. If a promotion rewards speed or volume, it works against everything the service policy asks staff to do. Look at each offer and ask whether it would make a server's job harder at 11 pm.

Small design choices help the other way. Put soft drinks, a good non-alcoholic beer and free drinking water on the menu where guests see them. Serve food until close, or close to it. Offer smaller serves of strong beers, such as a 200 ml glass for anything over 8% ABV. None of this costs much. All of it makes the amber stage easier to manage.

A policy works only if the team believes management will back them. If an owner overrules a manager to keep a big spender happy, the policy is dead from that night on. Say in writing that no staff member will be penalised for refusing service in good faith.

Train every new hire on the signs and the traffic lights in their first week. Role play the refusal conversation. It feels awkward in a quiet afternoon training session, which is exactly why it should happen then rather than at midnight. Our guide to a staff drinking policy covers the other half: staff who are sober can spot guests who are not.

Keep an incident book or a simple form: date, time, what happened, who handled it and what the outcome was. Note refusals as well as fights. Over a few months the log shows patterns. Maybe trouble clusters on one night, around one promotion or after a certain hour. That is the evidence you need to change a happy hour, add a security person or move last orders earlier.

A responsible service policy is one of the first documents a new brewpub should write, alongside the licence file and the food safety folder.
faqs: What is the drink driving limit in India?
The legal limit is 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood. One or two strong beers can take a guest over it, so offer a cab or driver.
Who should refuse service to a drunk guest?
The shift manager, privately and calmly. Junior servers should flag the guest to the manager rather than handle the refusal alone.
Is the legal drinking age the same across India?
No. It varies by state and the rules change, so check the current law where your brewpub operates and train staff to check ID.
